title: Tamil Shaivism and the Tevaram
hook: a locked room in a temple, a king outside the door, and palm leaves half eaten by ants: how tradition says the Tevaram came back

segments.voice: Yesterday closed a season: in their own words where they exist, ending with Karaikkal Ammaiyar, who signed her hymns as the pey of Karaikkal. Her songs sit in the same collection as the Tevaram. Today, that's where we go. Day one thousand three hundred seventy.

A sealed door in the great temple at Chidambaram, the temple of Shiva as the dancer. Behind it, tradition says, lies a room no one has opened in a very long time. Outside stands a Chola king. He has heard a few verses of the old Tamil hymns to Shiva sung at his court, and he wants the rest. The priests won't open the door for him. Only the singers who made these hymns, they say, can open it. And those singers are long gone. A new part of the path begins here: the regional traditions, starting in the Tamil south.
screen: `A SEALED DOOR AT CHIDAMBARAM.` → `A KING WHO WANTS THE HYMNS.` → `ONLY THE SINGERS CAN OPEN IT.`

segments.voice: Here's how the story goes, as tradition tells it, in paraphrase. The king won't be stopped. If only the saints can open the door, he'll bring the saints. He has images of the three singers, Appar, Sambandar and Sundarar, carried through the streets in procession and set before the room. The door is opened. Inside are the palm leaves the hymns were written on, and much of them has been eaten away by white ants. The king is heartbroken. Then, the story says, a voice is heard: what this age needs has been kept. A learned devotee, Nambi Andar Nambi, gathers what survives and sets it in order, and the hymns are sung again. That gathering is the Tevaram, and it stands at the heart of the Tirumurai, the sacred collection of Tamil Shaiva hymns. Now turn it. The story is about loss as much as rescue. It doesn't pretend nothing was lost. It says the ants got there first, and still, what was needed remained. Turn it again. Notice what the Tevaram is made of. These hymns are in Tamil, not Sanskrit, and they are tied to places. A hymn praises the Shiva of this town, by this river, in this grove of trees, with this temple tank. The singers walked from shrine to shrine and sang each one. So Tamil Shaivism is a faith with a map in its scripture. Turn it once more. The way the story imagines it, the key to the room was the singers themselves. Their words could only be opened by their presence. That's the ground a regional tradition stands on: Shiva, worshiped in a particular language, in particular places, through particular voices.
screen: `THE SAINTS CARRIED TO THE DOOR` · `PALM LEAVES EATEN BY ANTS` · `WHAT THIS AGE NEEDS WAS KEPT` · `HYMNS WITH A MAP INSIDE`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: what was kept. Sit, and let the breath slow. Bring to mind something that came to you only in part: a grandmother's recipe half remembered, a few words of a language, a song you know only the chorus of, a faith you were handed in pieces. Don't grieve the missing parts for now. Hold what remains. Let it be enough to sit with. If you pray, you can give thanks for what was kept. The bell holds the time.
Tamil Shaivism and the Tevaram. The Tamil hymns to Shiva of Appar, Sambandar and Sundarar, sung place by place, and, tradition says, rescued from a sealed room at Chidambaram. Today's word.
screen: `TAMIL SHAIVISM AND THE TEVARAM — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: Tamil Shaivism and the Tevaram. Today, ask someone older about one story or song you only know in part, and write down whatever they remember. Day one thousand three hundred seventy.

trapdoor: what you thought: a scripture is one old book, kept whole from the start.
what it means: tradition says the Tevaram was found half eaten by ants in a sealed room, and gathered from what survived.
what a scholar hears: a Tamil scripture tied to places, and a rescue story that admits loss: what this age needs was kept.
